headline: Sole developer on a national SSO platform for six months, with Claude writing most of the code
summary: A solution architect built a national Single Sign-On system for a Gulf country in six months, with AI assistant Claude generating the majority of the code. This project was estimated to require 3-4 engineers over three months without AI.
details: A solution architect was the sole hands-on developer for the identity and single-sign-on layer of a Gulf country's national port community system for six months. During this period, AI assistant Claude wrote approximately 70-80% of the backend and frontend code, enabling one developer to achieve what was estimated to require 3-4 engineers over three months.

The system was built with a hexagonal (ports and adapters) and CQRS architecture, ensuring clean separation of concerns. External dependencies were abstracted behind ports with mock adapters, allowing QA and UAT to run full end-to-end flows independently of unstable government systems.

The developer implemented optimistic locking with @Version to prevent duplicate-key errors in Spring Data and used the State pattern for user lifecycle management, ensuring invalid transitions fail at the domain layer. A manual metadata parser was written for malformed AVA encoding that the JDK's strict parser rejected.

When the ministry rotated its signing certificate in production, causing downtime, the developer made the certificate hot-reloadable with on-failure refresh. This allowed the system to self-heal during a subsequent rotation, preventing further outages.

Despite initial assumptions of network latency for India-Oman connections, the developer diagnosed unstable government APIs as the root cause of 500/503 errors, leading to the implementation of retry-with-backoff. A critical issue involved a production API returning 'WORKING' instead of 'Active' for work permits, silently blocking user registration.

Complex payment flow issues arose from mismatched timings between invoice expiry, frontend polling, and backend reconciliation, potentially causing successful payments to fail user-side. The solution involved two independent backend schedulers and dual finalization paths (bank callback and SPA polling) with an idempotency guard.

Other issues included a browser GET request silently dropping a POST body for a bank payment endpoint, fixed by a backend-rendered auto-submit form. Infrastructure configuration, not backend auth, caused API calls to fail while SAML redirects succeeded, leading to 16 distinct revert-and-rebuild cycles.

headline_marked: [[Lost Nintendo DS game cartridge hits eBay]] for $9,100, designed to self-delete after 12 hours
headline: Lost Nintendo DS game cartridge hits eBay for $9,100, designed to self-delete after 12 hours
summary: A one-of-a-kind development cartridge for the "PokePark Fishing Contest DS" minigame, previously considered lost media, is now up for auction on eBay with a starting bid of $9,100. The game was only distributed at a 2005 theme park and self-deleted.
details: A Nintendo DS game, "PokePark Fishing Contest DS," considered 'lost media' for nearly two decades, is now on eBay. An ultra-rare development cartridge, potentially one-of-a-kind, is listed with a starting bid of $9,100 (€7,999).

The minigame was exclusive to attendees of Japan's PokePark 2005 and distributed via DS Download Play. It was designed to be removed from a DS handheld after power-off or a 12-hour limit, making it incredibly difficult to archive.

Japanese game archaeology enthusiast Yoshino @ Federation highlighted the auction's significance. The eBay listing shows the large development and testing cartridge, along with an image of it working on a DS, displaying a high-score ranking communication program.
The Germany-based seller, catbearpaws, acquired the cart privately and is selling it "as-is" without guarantees on functionality or provenance. Bidding is active with less than three days remaining.

While the listing appears to confirm it's a dev cart for "PokePark Fishing Contest DS" assets, it's uncertain if a playable version can be extracted. This expensive artifact holds significant potential for retro gaming archivists.
